# Abstract

The southern tip of the Indian peninsula (167.458 km², encompassing 1.989 active 5-arcminute terrestrial cells) supported one of the most continuous agrarian civilisations in the pre-modern world. Extending from the forested escarpments of the Western Ghats to the Coromandel coast and the Malabar littoral, Tamil Nadu and Kerala developed distinct regional modes of hydraulic adaptation, civic organisation and commercial exchange between 300AD and 1526AD. Reconstructed across three physiographic divisions under INDUS, regional population expanded from 5,10M inhabitants in 300AD during late antiquity to 6,20M in 600AD as early mediaeval agrarian kingdoms consolidated in the river valleys. Demographic growth quickened under the Pallavas and Early Pandyas, reaching 7,80M in 900AD, before accelerating under the Imperial Cholas to 9,40M in 1050AD and attaining 10,40M in 1200AD. Following the thirteenth-century resurgence of the Second Pandya Empire and the expansion of the Vijayanagara Empire into the Tamil plains, regional population climbed to 11,20M in 1350AD and reached 12,80M by 1526AD, yielding an aggregate demographic density of 76,44 persons per km² (7.643,71 persons per 100 km²). This demographic expansion was sustained by the construction of cascading tank networks (*eri*) in dry uplands, deltaic canal diversion along the Kaveri, institutional management through *brahmadeya* and *ur* assemblies, temple urbanism and trans-oceanic spice commerce connecting Malabar and Coromandel ports to the wider Indian Ocean.

# Background

## Fluvial Ecology, Monsoonal Regimes and Regional Topography

The physical geography of southern South Asia is defined by the sharp climatic barrier of the Western Ghats, an unbroken crystalline ridge extending parallel to the Arabian Sea [@Shanmugasundaram2017North]. The range bisects the macro-region into two hydroclimatic zones: a narrow, humid western coastal strip comprising Kerala (Malabar), receiving between 2.500 mm and 3.500 mm of annual rainfall from the southwest monsoon, and a broad, semi-arid eastern plain comprising Tamil Nadu, shielded by the mountains from summer rains and reliant primarily on the northeast monsoon between October and December [@Shanmugasundaram2017North].

In Tamil Nadu, river systems originate in the eastern slopes of the Ghats and flow eastward into the Bay of Bengal [@Rita2022River]. The Kaveri River forms the primary agricultural artery of the southern peninsula. Emerging from Coorg, it traverses the Karnataka plateau before descending through the granite gorge of Hogenakkal into the Tamil lowlands, where it receives major tributaries including the Bhavani, Amaravati and Noyyal across Kongu Nadu [@Guahk2022Recovering]. Below Tiruchirappalli, the river branches into the Coleroon (Kollidam) and the Kaveri proper, forming an expansive delta fan whose fertile alluvial deposits provided the economic foundation for the Imperial Chola state [@SHOBA2022Cholas]. North of the Kaveri basin, the Palar, Cheyyar and Pennaiyar drain the granitic plateau of Tondaimandalam, sustaining extensive irrigated agriculture through seasonal stream diversions. South of the Kaveri delta, the Vaigai and Tambraparani rivers flow through the semi-arid plains of Pandya Nadu, where ancient bunding and weir engineering supported dense agrarian populations around Madurai and Tirunelveli [@Mandal2026Water].

In Kerala, the drainage landscape consists of forty-one short, fast-flowing coastal rivers that debouch into the Arabian Sea through a complex system of interconnected brackish lagoons and backwaters (*kayals*) [@Rita2022River]. The Periyar and the Bharathappuzha (Nila) provided natural transport conduits between the spice-producing highland forests of the Anamalai and Cardamom hills and the maritime emporia of the littoral, including Kodungallur (Muziris), Kozhikode (Calicut) and Kollam (Quilon) [@Kooria2022Encounters; @S2021Historical]. The Palghat Gap, a 30 km wide tectonic break in the Western Ghats, formed the sole low-altitude overland transit corridor connecting the Malabar coast directly to the inland Tamil plains of Kongu Nadu, facilitating commercial caravans and military campaigns throughout historical times [@Paleri2023Elections].

## Late Sangam Legacy, Kalabhra Transition and Early Agrarian Nucleation

During the early centuries of the common era, southern India was characterised by the commercial networks of the Sangam era, wherein coastal ports such as Kaveripattinam (Poompuhar) at the mouth of the Kaveri, Korkai on the Gulf of Mannar, Arikamedu near Puducherry and Muziris (Pattanam) in Kerala mediated lucrative maritime trade with the Roman Empire and the Mediterranean basin [@S2021Historical; @Mathar2025Echoes]. Sangam poetic anthologies classify the landscape into five ecological zones (*tinai*): coastal tracts (*neital*), riverine agricultural lowlands (*marutam*), pastoral scrublands (*mullai*), dry scrub deserts (*palai*) and forested hills (*kurinji*).

Between 300AD and 600AD, the classical Sangam chiefdoms dissolved during what later Brahmanical epigraphy termed the Kalabhra interregnum [@Kulke2009Bibliograp]. Far from representing a destructive dark age, this transition marked the initial institutional expansion of settled agriculture outside the narrow coastal deltas into the interior dry plains [@Gunasekaran2026Power]. Non-Brahmanical religious orders, predominantly Jainism and Buddhism, flourished across Tamil cities during this period, leaving architectural and epigraphic imprints at Madurai, Kanchipuram and Kaveripattinam [@Cox2016Conclusion]. The Kalabhra era stimulated early wet-rice settlement expansion and communal tank construction that prepared the ground for the dynastic resurgence of the sixth century [@Mandal2026Water].

## Pallava and Early Pandya State Formation

From the late sixth century, two powerful dynasties reorganised the agrarian and political landscape of the Tamil country: the Pallavas of Kanchipuram in the north and the Early Pandyas of Madurai in the south [@Kumar2024Architectu; @Journal2025]. The Pallava rulers, beginning with Simhavishnu (ca. 575AD-600AD) and Mahendravarman I (ca. 600AD-630AD), established royal control over Tondaimandalam and the lower Palar basin. Mahendravarman I pioneered rock-cut cave temples carved directly into granite outcrops at Mandagapattu, Mamallapuram and Tiruchirappalli, initiating an architectural tradition that transformed the ritual landscape [@Kumar2024Architectu]. Under Narasimhavarman I and Rajasimha, the Pallavas developed Mamallapuram into a fortified port city and diplomatic gateway to Southeast Asia, while constructing monumental structural temples such as the Kailasanatha at Kanchipuram and the Shore Temple at Mamallapuram [@Careem2024Goddesses].

Simultaneously, the Early Pandyas, revived under Kadungon (ca. 590AD-620AD), established their authority across the southern Tamil plains from their ancient capital at Madurai on the Vaigai River [@Journal2025]. Pandya epigraphy documents royal endowments to Saiva and Vaishnava shrines, coinciding with the popular *bhakti* devotional movement led by the Nayanars and Alvars. This religious revival forged close institutional linkages between agrarian temple networks and royal legitimacy [@Trouillet2017Hindu]. Across the Western Ghats, the Chera Perumals established a unified monarchy based at Mahodayapuram (Kodungallur), coordinating agrarian estates and granting royal protection charters to Jewish, Syrian Christian and Arab trading communities at Kollam and Muziris [@Kooria2022Encounters; @S2021Historical; @Champakalakshmi1996Trade].

## Imperial Chola Hegemony and Hydraulic Tank Systems

The ninth century witnessed the dramatic re-emergence of the Cholas under Vijayalaya (ca. 850AD-870AD), who seized Thanjavur from the Muttaraiyar chieftains and established it as the dynastic capital [@Mala2025Agricultur]. Over the subsequent three centuries, the Imperial Cholas created the most centralised agrarian state in pre-modern southern India, reaching their political and demographic apex under Rajaraja I (985AD-1014AD) and his son Rajendra I (1012AD-1044AD) [@Mala2025Agricultur; @SHOBA2022Cholas].

The Chola agrarian state was anchored by two complementary village institutions documented across thousands of stone inscriptions:
1. The *ur*, the assembly of peasant cultivators (*vellanvagai*), which managed communal lands, assessed local grain dues and allocated seasonal irrigation water [@Mala2025Agricultur].
2. The *sabha* or *mahasabha*, the corporate assembly of Brahman landholders in tax-exempt settlement colonies (*brahmadeya*), which supervised complex multi-village irrigation systems, administered civil justice and coordinated temple construction [@Ridisha2026Contributi].

At Uthiramerur in Tondaimandalam, tenth-century inscriptional records describe the detailed democratic operation of the village *sabha*, including the election of executive committees (*variyams*) responsible for tank maintenance (*eri-variyam*), agricultural garden lands (*totta-variyam*) and annual revenue collection (*pancha-vara-variyam*) through a secret pot-ballot system (*kudavolai*) [@Ridisha2026Contributi].

Chola hydraulic engineering attained an unprecedented scale. Across the Kaveri delta, state engineers constructed masonry anicuts (diversion weirs) to divide river channels into an intricate lattice of distributary canals, including the Grand Anicut (Kallanai), originally attributed to early rulers but extensively raised and reinforced during the Imperial Chola epoch [@SHOBA2022Cholas]. In upland rainfed districts, communities excavated cascading chains of earthen irrigation tanks (*eri*). These reservoirs captured seasonal monsoon runoff and channelled it from higher to lower tanks through masonry sluices (*madagu*), ensuring that excess overflow in upstream catchments was stored rather than lost to coastal drainage [@Mandal2026Water]. Rajendra I commemorated his northern military campaigns to the Ganges by constructing the monumental *Chola-gangam* reservoir (Ponneri) at his new imperial capital of Gangaikonda Cholapuram, creating an artificial lake exceeding 25 km in perimeter to irrigate surrounding drylands [@Thamilarasi2024Architectu].

Monumental temple complexes, exemplified by the Brihadisvara at Thanjavur and the Gangaikonda Cholisvaram, functioned as economic redistribution centres [@Kala2021Saranathap; @Champakalakshmi1996Trade]. Temples held vast agrarian estates (*devadana*), employed thousands of priests, musicians, artisans and agricultural tenants, operated as rural credit banks lending capital at fixed grain interest, and stimulated regional market towns (*nagaram*) where merchant guilds traded local and imported commodities [@Trouillet2017Hindu; @Gurevitch2026Handmade; @Champakalakshmi1996Trade]. Chola naval expeditions across the Bay of Bengal to the Srivijaya Empire in Sumatra and Malaya protected oceanic trade corridors utilised by powerful commercial corporations such as the *Ayyavole 500* (Ainnurruvar) and the *Manigramam*, who exported textiles, spices and bronzes to Song China [@Careem2024Goddesses; @Kulke2009Bibliograp; @Chattopadhyaya1994Making].

## Pandya Resurgence, Hoysala Entanglements and Malabar Maritime Hubs

During the thirteenth century, Chola imperial power declined under pressure from external invasions and internal regional centrifugal forces [@Bes2022Introducti]. The Second Pandya Empire, revived under Maravarman Sundara Pandya I (1216AD-1238AD) and Jatavarman Sundara Pandya I (1251AD-1268AD), defeated the later Cholas and annexed Thanjavur, establishing Madurai as the supreme political capital of the Tamil country [@Journal2025; @RamadeviSekhar2026Inheritanc]. Pandya authority was contested by the Hoysala dynasty of the Karnataka plateau, who established a secondary southern capital at Kannanur Kupam (Samayapuram) near Srirangam to control the wealth of the Kaveri delta [@KN2026Epigraphs].

This era of intense inter-dynastic conflict is attested by hundreds of commemorative hero stones (*natukal*) erected across Tamil Nadu and southern Karnataka, recording village defense skirmishes, cattle raids and border warfare [@Ali2025Rural; @Babu2024Memories]. Despite military instability, agricultural property rights expanded. Inscriptions from the thirteenth century document increasing individual land ownership, female inheritance rights and active private land sales in the Kaveri and Vaigai basins [@RamadeviSekhar2026Inheritanc].

In Kerala, the collapse of the Chera Perumal central monarchy around 1102AD produced a mosaic of autonomous feudal principalities (*svarupams*), among which the Samoothiri (Zamorin) of Kozhikode (Calicut), the Kolathiri of Kannur and the Venad rajas of Kollam emerged as the dominant powers [@Paleri2023Elections; @Bes2022Introducti]. Kozhikode developed into the premier oceanic transshipment port of the Indian Ocean spice trade, where Muslim merchant shipmasters (*nakhudas*), Chinese treasure fleets and Gujarati traders bartered Malabar black pepper, ginger and cardamom for Persian horses, Arabian perfumes and Chinese porcelain [@Kooria2022Encounters].

## The Madurai Sultanate and Vijayanagara Consolidation

In 1311AD, the southern peninsula was invaded by the Delhi Sultanate army led by Malik Kafur, who plundered temple wealth at Kanchipuram, Srirangam, Madurai and Chidambaram [@Eaton2019India]. Following subsequent campaigns by Muhammad bin Tughluq, the Delhi governor Jalaluddin Ahsan Khan declared independence in 1335AD, establishing the short-lived Madurai Sultanate [@Eaton2019India; @Careem2024Goddesses]. The Sultanate ruled the southern Tamil plains for four decades until its overthrow in 1378AD by the forces of the Vijayanagara Empire, commanded by Prince Kumara Kampana [@Eaton2019India].

The incorporation of Tamil Nadu into the Vijayanagara Empire ushered in sweeping socio-economic and demographic changes [@Bes2022Heirs; @Stein1989Vijayanagara]. Vijayanagara emperors divided the Tamil territories among military governors (*nayakas*), who established prominent regional courts at Senji (Gingee), Thanjavur and Madurai [@Bes2022Heirs; @Bes2022Sources; @Stein1989Vijayanagara]. The Nayaka administration encouraged large-scale migration of Telugu warrior and agrarian lineages (*Nayakas*, *Reddis*, *Kammavars*) into the semi-arid interior tracts of Kongu Nadu, Tirunelveli and Ramanathapuram [@Gunasekaran2026Power; @Stein1989Vijayanagara]. These settlers cleared dry scrub forests (*kadu-vetti-nadu-akkal*), introduced deep well irrigation using leather bucket lifters (*kavalai*), and cultivated dry cash crops including cotton, indigo, millets and oilseeds [@Gunasekaran2026Power; @Gurevitch2026Handmade]. Massive stone fortifications were erected at Senji, Vellore and Chandragiri to secure trade routes and frontier passes [@Rakesh2022Forts]. Monumental architectural additions, particularly towering multi-tiered entrance gateways (*rayagopurams*) and thousand-pillared mandapas, were constructed across major shrines at Tirupati, Madurai, Srirangam, Chidambaram and Tiruvannamalai, consolidating urban populations around temple centres [@Kumar2024Architectu; @Udayakumar2019Architectu; @Stein1989Vijayanagara].

# Methodology

## Spatial Grid Partition and Environmental Covariates

To model demographic distributions across 167.458 km² of peninsular territory, the INDUS spatial framework partitions Tamil Nadu and Kerala into 1.989 active 5-arcminute terrestrial grid cells (measuring approximately 9,2 km by 9,2 km). Each cell is evaluated against environmental covariates:
- Fluvial distance decay: proximity to perennial rivers (Kaveri, Palar, Vaigai, Tambraparani, Periyar, Bharathappuzha), with exponential density attenuation beyond 12 km in dry interior zones [@Rita2022River; @Guahk2022Recovering].
- Monsoonal precipitation gradients: continuous weighting calibrated to regional rain gauge and palaeoclimate moisture models, distinguishing wet Malabar and Coromandel coastal zones from the rain-shadow tracts of the interior plateau [@Shanmugasundaram2017North].
- Topographic slope: penalising rugged crystalline escarpments of the Western Ghats (Nilgiris, Anamalais, Cardamom Hills) while favouring broad alluvial fans, deltaic lowlands and coastal plains.
- Soil suitability: incorporating regional pedological classifications, giving highest weight to Kaveri alluvial silts, followed by deep black regur soils in Kongu Nadu and Tirunelveli, and lower weights to lateritic upland soils [@Mala2025Agricultur].

## Settlement Subtraction and Rural Dasymetric Allocation

To prevent demographic double counting between nucleated urban centres and rural agricultural populations, 3.855 catalogued settlements (1.879 in Pallava Tondaimandalam, Chola Kaveri and Kongu; 1.045 in Chera Perumal, Venad and Calicut Malabar; and 931 in Pandya Nadu and the southern Tamil plains) with continuous or benchmark demographic trajectories are anchored to their WGS84 geographic coordinates. At each benchmark year (300AD, 600AD, 900AD, 1050AD, 1200AD, 1350AD and 1526AD), the summed population of all catalogued settlements within each sub-region is subtracted from the sub-regional population total.

The residual rural population is then allocated across non-settled terrestrial grid cells in proportion to environmental suitability weights. A boundary feathering filter smoothes density transitions across sub-regional borders, avoiding artificial step discontinuities along administrative divides.

## Demographic Envelopes and Sub-Regional Densities

Sub-regional demographic estimates are bounded by explicit uncertainty intervals reflecting variations in epigraphic visibility, urban room counts and historical crop yield estimates. Across the seven benchmark periods, sub-regional estimates carry an uncertainty margin of +/- 10% to +/- 12%. Table \ref{tab:subregions} documents the three sub-regions, land areas, benchmark population trajectories and 1526AD demographic densities.

```{r tbl-subregions, results='asis'}
sub_rows <- lapply(reg_keys, function (rk) {
  r <- mod_data$regions[[rk]]
  a <- as.numeric(r$area_km2)
  p_300 <- as.numeric(r$population[["300"]])
  p_600 <- as.numeric(r$population[["600"]])
  p_900 <- as.numeric(r$population[["900"]])
  p_1050 <- as.numeric(r$population[["1050"]])
  p_1200 <- as.numeric(r$population[["1200"]])
  p_1350 <- as.numeric(r$population[["1350"]])
  p_1526 <- as.numeric(r$population[["1526"]])
  dens_1526 <- p_1526 / a * 100
  data.frame(
    Region = if (!is.null(reg_short[[rk]])) reg_short[[rk]] else clean_text(r$name),
    Area = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(a, 0L), " (", viscount_fmt_number(a / tot_area * 100, 1L), "%)"),
    P300AD = viscount_fmt_pop(p_300),
    P600AD = viscount_fmt_pop(p_600),
    P900AD = viscount_fmt_pop(p_900),
    P1050AD = viscount_fmt_pop(p_1050),
    P1200AD = viscount_fmt_pop(p_1200),
    P1350AD = viscount_fmt_pop(p_1350),
    P1526AD = viscount_fmt_pop(p_1526),
    Density1526 = viscount_fmt_number(dens_1526, 2L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_sub <- do.call(rbind, sub_rows)
df_tot <- data.frame(
  Region = "Regional Total",
  Area = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(tot_area, 0L), " (100%)"),
  P300AD = viscount_fmt_pop(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["300"]]),
  P600AD = viscount_fmt_pop(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["600"]]),
  P900AD = viscount_fmt_pop(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["900"]]),
  P1050AD = viscount_fmt_pop(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["1050"]]),
  P1200AD = viscount_fmt_pop(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["1200"]]),
  P1350AD = viscount_fmt_pop(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["1350"]]),
  P1526AD = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_1526),
  Density1526 = viscount_fmt_number(tot_1526 / tot_area * 100, 2L),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
df_sub <- rbind(df_sub, df_tot)
viscount_table(
  df_sub,
  "Sub-regional land area, benchmark populations and 1526AD density across Tamil Nadu and Kerala.",
  c("Sub-Region", "Area km² (Share)", "300AD", "600AD", "900AD", "1050AD", "1200AD", "1350AD", "1526AD", "1526AD Density"),
  list(label = "tab:subregions", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

# Testing and Validation

## Epigraphic Density and Inscriptional Land Grant Surveys

Demographic distributions across Tamil Nadu and Kerala are validated against over 25.000 published stone inscriptions catalogued in *South Indian Inscriptions*, *Epigraphia Indica* and regional epigraphic volumes [@Shin2024Claiming; @THALINJA2026Rare]. Spatial mapping of inscriptional find-spots reveals an overwhelming concentration in the Kaveri delta (Thanjavur, Tiruchirappalli, Nagapattinam), followed by Tondaimandalam (Kanchipuram, Chengalpattu) and the Vaigai-Tambraparani basins (Madurai, Tirunelveli) [@Cox2016Conclusion; @Udayakumar2019Architectu].

This inscriptional density directly reflects historical settlement concentration:
- In the Kaveri delta, an average of 4,2 inscriptions per square kilometre survive from the Chola epoch, attesting to dense village corporate governance and continuous hydraulic investment [@Mala2025Agricultur; @Thamilarasi2024Architectu].
- In Tondaimandalam, inscriptional records average 2,1 per square kilometre, dominated by tank construction and maintenance charters by village assemblies [@Ridisha2026Contributi].
- In Pandya Nadu, records average 1,8 per square kilometre, reflecting royal land donations to temple foundations and hero-stone commemorations along frontier routes [@Ali2025Rural; @Journal2025].
- In Kerala, where historical documents were predominantly inscribed on perishable palm leaves (*oles*), stone temple inscriptions and copper-plate grants (*shasanams*) provide vital chronological benchmarks for urban settlements at Kodungallur, Kollam and Kozhikode [@Kooria2022Encounters; @S2021Historical].

## Hydroclimatic Calibration and Northeast Monsoon Variability

Palaeoclimatic proxy records derived from speleothems, tree rings and sediment cores across southern peninsular India confirm long-term variations in monsoonal precipitation [@Shanmugasundaram2017North]. The Mediaeval Warm Period (ca. 900AD to 1250AD) coincided with an enhanced northeast monsoon regime over the Coromandel coast, delivering regular winter rainfall that filled cascading tank networks and recharged groundwater tables across Tamil Nadu [@Mandal2026Water]. This hydroclimatic phase coincided precisely with the golden age of Imperial Chola agrarian expansion and temple construction [@SHOBA2022Cholas].

Conversely, the onset of the Little Ice Age during the fourteenth century caused increased rainfall variability, characterised by erratic monsoons and localized droughts [@Shanmugasundaram2017North]. The agrarian reorganisation undertaken by Vijayanagara nayakas, specifically the expansion of deep-well irrigation (*kavalai*) and dryland crop diversification (millets, cotton, oilseeds), constituted an adaptive agricultural response to these climatic fluctuations [@Gunasekaran2026Power; @Gurevitch2026Handmade].

## Agricultural Multi-Cropping and Tank Hydraulic Capacity

Agronomic data from epigraphic revenue surveys confirm that mediaeval Tamil agriculture achieved high caloric yields through dual-season cropping [@Mala2025Agricultur; @SHOBA2022Cholas]. In the Kaveri delta, farmers practiced double-cropping of wet rice:
- The *kuruvai* crop (short-duration rice), planted in June-July and harvested in October, nourished by southwest monsoon river freshes.
- The *samba* crop (long-duration rice), planted in August-September and harvested in January-February, nurtured by the heavy rains of the northeast monsoon.

In rainfed upland districts, cascading tank chains (*eri*) stored between 150.000 m³ and 2,5M m³ of runoff per tank [@Mandal2026Water]. Hydraulic analysis demonstrates that a standard cascading chain of ten to fifteen tanks could insulate between 800 ha and 1.500 ha of wet paddy land against seasonal rain deficits, supporting village demographic densities of 180 to 250 persons per km² in tracts where natural rainfall did not exceed 750 mm annually [@SHOBA2022Cholas; @Mandal2026Water].

In Kerala, double-cropping of wet paddy in alluvial valley bottoms (*kandam*) was complemented by intensive multi-tier tree horticulture on coastal and hillside terraces (*parambu*), combining coconut palms, areca nuts, black pepper vines, jackfruit and bananas [@Kooria2022Encounters]. This agrarian regime supported sustained population densities along the Malabar coastal strip without requiring extensive canal works.

## Source Ledger Ingestion and Saturation Audit

The INDUS source ledger was constructed through a four-wave asymptotic ingestion process designed to capture all nucleated settlement nodes across primary historical monographs, multi-repository archaeological corpora and official censuses [@Champakalakshmi1996Trade; @Stein1989Vijayanagara; @ImperialGazetteer1908]:
- Wave 1: Systematic ingestion of official national census registers (including Census of India Table A-04 sub-district series), imperial gazetteer anchors and primary-monograph city trajectories, establishing 2.236 georeferenced settlements [@ImperialGazetteer1908; @Habib1982Atlas].
- Wave 2: Extraction of historical localities from multi-repository archaeological and monument corpora (Pleiades, Archaeological Survey of India P1371, Zenodo regional surveys, Wikidata, OpenStreetMap and radiocarbon compendia), adding 1.079 settlements [@Allchin1995Archaeology; @Erdosy1988Urbanisation].
- Wave 3: Macro-envelope *qasba*, *pargana* and *nadu* continuity reconciliation and longitudinal foundation-year audits, capturing 540 ancient and early mediaeval sites [@Chattopadhyaya1994Making; @Hambly1982Towns].
- Wave 4: Sub-mask gap hunting and GeoNames homonym audits across all three divisions, confirming asymptotic saturation with zero newly included localities (marginal gain 0,0%).

In total, 4.655 candidate localities were audited: 3.855 were accepted as primary catalogued settlements (1.879 in Tondaimandalam and Chola Kaveri, 1.045 in Malabar and 931 in Pandya Nadu) and 800 were excluded (predominantly duplicate aliases within a 2,2 km deduplication radius or non-habitation architectural features).

# Results

## Demographic Trajectory and Benchmark Analysis

The demographic trajectory of Tamil Nadu and Kerala from 300AD to 1526AD exhibits steady, cumulative growth punctuated by two major accelerations: the Imperial Chola agrarian zenith between 900AD and 1200AD, and the Vijayanagara dryland expansion between 1350AD and 1526AD (Figure \ref{fig:trajectory} and Table \ref{tab:benchmarks}).

```{r fig-trajectory, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/fig2_tamil_nadu_and_kerala_until_mughal_empire_demography.png",
  "Long-term demographic trajectory of Tamil Nadu and Kerala (300AD to 1526AD), showing benchmark population growth across three sub-regions, Imperial Chola apex and Vijayanagara expansion.",
  "fig:trajectory"
)
```

```{r tbl-benchmarks, results='asis'}
bm_years <- c("300", "600", "900", "1050", "1200", "1350", "1526")
bm_rows <- lapply(bm_years, function (yk) {
  tot_pop <- as.numeric(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[[yk]])
  mal <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$tam2_malabar_perumal$population[[yk]])
  ton <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$tam2_tondai_chola$population[[yk]])
  pan <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$tam2_pandya_madurai$population[[yk]])
  dens <- tot_pop / tot_area * 100
  data.frame(
    Benchmark = fmt_yr(yk),
    TotalPop = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_pop),
    Density = viscount_fmt_number(dens, 2L),
    TondaiChola = viscount_fmt_pop(ton),
    Malabar = viscount_fmt_pop(mal),
    PandyaNadu = viscount_fmt_pop(pan),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_bm <- do.call(rbind, bm_rows)
viscount_table(
  df_bm,
  "Benchmark population totals and sub-regional distribution across Tamil Nadu and Kerala (300AD to 1526AD).",
  c("Benchmark", "Regional Pop", "Density", "Tondaimandalam and Chola", "Malabar and Perumal", "Pandya Nadu"),
  list(label = "tab:benchmarks", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

## Historical Demographic Epochs

### Late Antiquity and Early Mediaeval Transition (300AD to 600AD)

Between 300AD and 600AD, regional population increased from 5,10M to 6,20M inhabitants (an annual growth rate of 0,065%), while aggregate density rose from 30,46 to 37,02 persons per km². Following the decline of Roman maritime trade, demographic mass reoriented from coastal trading stations such as Kaveripattinam (32k in 300AD), Pattanam (22k in 300AD), Korkai (18k in 300AD) and Arikamedu (10k in 300AD) toward inland riverine valleys [@S2021Historical; @Mathar2025Echoes; @Allchin1995Archaeology]. During the Kalabhra period, initial wet-rice expansion took root in the lower Kaveri and Palar basins, supporting major interior centres at Madurai (45k in 300AD to 55k in 600AD), Kanchipuram (42,71k in 300AD to 75k in 600AD) and Tiruchirappalli (34,96k in 300AD to 32k in 600AD), and laying the institutional groundwork for subsequent dynastic consolidation [@Gunasekaran2026Power; @Erdosy1988Urbanisation].

### Pallava, Early Pandya and Chera Perumal Consolidation (600AD to 900AD)

The three centuries from 600AD to 900AD witnessed sustained population growth, reaching 7,80M by 900AD (yielding an aggregate density of 46,58 persons per km²). The Pallavas developed Tondaimandalam into an intensively cultivated agrarian core, creating major civic and sacred centres at Kanchipuram (peaking at 83,55k in 700AD and holding 78k in 900AD) and Tiruchirappalli (38k in 900AD) [@Kumar2024Architectu; @Champakalakshmi1996Trade]. In Pandya Nadu, population reached 2,11M in 900AD, anchored by Madurai (65k in 900AD) on the Vaigai River and Thanjavur (55k in 900AD) on the edge of the Kaveri delta [@Journal2025; @Chattopadhyaya1994Making]. In Kerala, the Chera Perumals consolidated power at Mahodayapuram (Kodungallur, 32,62k in 900AD), while Kollam (20,1k in 900AD) emerged as a major Indian Ocean entrepôt [@Kooria2022Encounters].

### Imperial Chola Hegemony and Agrarian Zenith (900AD to 1200AD)

Between 900AD and 1200AD, the Imperial Cholas presided over the most dramatic phase of agrarian and demographic expansion in southern Indian history [@Mala2025Agricultur; @SHOBA2022Cholas; @Champakalakshmi1996Trade]. Regional population climbed to 9,40M in 1050AD and reached 10,40M by 1200AD (yielding an aggregate density of 62,11 persons per km²).

The demographic core was centred on the Kaveri delta and Tondaimandalam, where population reached 4,68M in 1200AD (45,0% of the regional total; 55,10 persons per km²):
- Thanjavur expanded into an imperial metropolis housing 95k inhabitants at its 1000AD peak (85k in 1050AD and 75k in 1200AD), coordinating regional grain revenue and artisan production [@Kala2021Saranathap; @Champakalakshmi1996Trade].
- Gangaikonda Cholapuram, founded by Rajendra I, housed 75k residents at its 1050AD apex (55k in 1200AD), supported by the massive *Chola-gangam* reservoir [@Thamilarasi2024Architectu].
- Kanchipuram remained a premier weaving and monastic hub (82k in 1050AD and 75k in 1200AD), complemented by Kumbakonam (38k in 1050AD and 36k in 1200AD) and Nagapattinam (35k peak in 1050AD and 32,73k in 1200AD), the foremost trans-oceanic port on the Coromandel coast [@Careem2024Goddesses; @Champakalakshmi1996Trade].

In Pandya Nadu, population expanded to 2,81M in 1200AD as Madurai reached its historical apex of 80,39k, while Malabar grew to 2,91M, supported by maritime trade at Kodungallur (peaking at 36,47k in 1000AD and holding 28k in 1200AD) and Kollam (33,84k in 1200AD) [@S2021Historical; @Kooria2022Encounters].

### Late Mediaeval Incursions, Pandya Climax and Calicut Spice Trade (1200AD to 1350AD)

Between 1200AD and 1350AD, population growth moderated, rising from 10,40M to 11,20M inhabitants (66,88 persons per km²). The Second Pandya Empire established political dominance over the Tamil plains, sustaining urban populations at Madurai (80,39k in 1200AD and 62k in 1350AD), Thanjavur (55k in 1350AD) and Tiruchirappalli (48k in 1200AD and 45k in 1350AD), even as Gangaikonda Cholapuram contracted sharply to 6k by 1350AD [@Journal2025; @RamadeviSekhar2026Inheritanc]. In Malabar, the disintegration of the Chera Perumal monarchy fostered the commercial rise of Kozhikode (Calicut) under the Zamorin, which grew from 22,85k in 1200AD to 46,4k inhabitants by 1350AD as the preeminent pepper entrepôt of the Arabian Sea, alongside Kollam at its 1350AD peak of 42k and the emerging harbour at Kochi (14k in 1350AD) [@Paleri2023Elections; @Bes2022Introducti]. The Delhi Sultanate incursions and the four-decade Madurai Sultanate disrupted traditional royal patronage but did not diminish aggregate agrarian capacity [@Eaton2019India].

### Vijayanagara Expansion and Nayaka Agrarian Reorganisation (1350AD to 1526AD)

From 1350AD to 1526AD, the integration of Tamil Nadu into the Vijayanagara Empire stimulated a second major demographic acceleration [@Bes2022Heirs; @Stein1989Vijayanagara]. Regional population expanded from 11,20M to 12,80M by 1526AD (yielding an aggregate density of 76,44 persons per km²).

Under the administration of the Vijayanagara nayakas at Senji (28k in 1526AD), Thanjavur and Madurai, massive agrarian colonisation was directed into the semi-arid interior scrublands of Kongu Nadu, Tirunelveli (30k in 1526AD) and Ramanathapuram [@Gunasekaran2026Power; @Stein1989Vijayanagara]. Telugu migrant lineages (*Kammavars*, *Reddis*) introduced deep-well irrigation (*kavalai*) and dryland multi-cropping, turning dry uplands into productive cotton, oilseed and millet belts [@Gunasekaran2026Power; @Gurevitch2026Handmade]. Urban centres coalesced around monumental temple cities with towering *rayagopurams*, including Madurai (72k in 1526AD), Kanchipuram (72k), Thanjavur (65k), Tiruchirappalli (55k peak in 1526AD) and the pilgrimage metropolis of Tirupati (48k peak in 1526AD) [@Kumar2024Architectu; @Bes2022Sources; @Stein1989Vijayanagara]. In Malabar, population climbed to 3,58M in 1526AD, anchored by Kozhikode (peaking at 74,78k in 1500AD and holding 72k in 1526AD), Kochi (42,6k peak in 1526AD), Kollam (36,57k) and Kannur (26,57k peak in 1526AD), which resisted Vijayanagara conquest while confronting the initial arrival of Portuguese maritime forces in 1498AD [@Kooria2022Encounters].

## Urban Hierarchy and Settlement Dynamics

Table \ref{tab:leading_settlements} presents the leading fifteen catalogued settlements across Tamil Nadu and Kerala ordered by peak population.

```{r tbl-leading-settlements, results='asis'}
set_list <- unname(set_data)
sett_peaks <- vapply(set_list, function (s) {
  if (is.null(s$population) || length(s$population) == 0) return(0)
  max(as.numeric(unlist(s$population)))
}, numeric(1))

ord <- order(sett_peaks, decreasing = TRUE)
top_sett <- set_list[ord]

top_rows <- lapply(head(top_sett, 15), function (s) {
  p_max <- max(as.numeric(unlist(s$population)))
  p_1200 <- if (!is.null(s$population[["1200"]])) as.numeric(s$population[["1200"]]) else "-"
  lat <- as.numeric(s$coords[[1]])
  lon <- as.numeric(s$coords[[2]])
  coord_str <- paste0(viscount_fmt_number(abs(lat), 2L), if (lat >= 0) " N" else " S", ", ",
                      viscount_fmt_number(abs(lon), 2L), if (lon >= 0) " E" else " W")
  reg_key <- if (!is.null(s$region_id)) s$region_id else s$region
  reg_lbl <- if (!is.null(reg_short[[reg_key]])) reg_short[[reg_key]] else clean_text(s$region)
  data.frame(
    Name = clean_text(s$name),
    SubRegion = reg_lbl,
    Coordinates = coord_str,
    PeakPop = viscount_fmt_pop(p_max),
    P1200AD = if (is.numeric(p_1200)) viscount_fmt_pop(p_1200) else "-",
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_top <- do.call(rbind, top_rows)
viscount_table(
  df_top,
  "Leading fifteen historical settlements across Tamil Nadu and Kerala, showing coordinates, peak population and 1200AD population.",
  c("Settlement Name", "Sub-Region", "Coordinates", "Peak Pop", "1200AD Pop"),
  list(label = "tab:leading_settlements", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

Across the 3.855 catalogued settlements, the regional rank-size distribution conforms closely to a Zipf power law with exponent $\alpha = 0,94$ ($R^2 = 0,95$), reflecting an integrated multi-tier urban hierarchy connecting deltaic capitals, inland temple centres and coastal ports. This historical hierarchy comprised four functional tiers:
1. Imperial and dynastic metropolises (> 70k inhabitants): Thanjavur (95k peak in 1000AD), the Chola capital commanding the Kaveri delta; Kanchipuram (83,55k peak in 700AD), the Pallava capital and silk-weaving centre; Madurai (80,39k peak in 1200AD), the enduring Pandya capital on the Vaigai River; Gangaikonda Cholapuram (75k peak in 1050AD), Rajendra I's imperial foundation; and Kozhikode (74,78k peak in 1500AD), the preeminent Malabar pepper entrepôt [@Kala2021Saranathap; @Champakalakshmi1996Trade; @Journal2025].
2. Major administrative, pilgrimage and maritime centres (40k to 70k inhabitants): Tiruchirappalli (55k peak in 1526AD) guarding the Kaveri bifurcation, Tirupati (48k peak in 1526AD), the major Vijayanagara shrine city, Kochi (42,6k peak in 1526AD) and Kollam (42k peak in 1350AD) [@Thamilarasi2024Architectu; @Stein1989Vijayanagara; @Bes2022Introducti].
3. Secondary ports and regional capitals (25k to 40k inhabitants): Kumbakonam (38k peak in 1050AD and 1526AD), Kodungallur (Muziris or Mahodayapuram, 36,47k peak in 1000AD), Nagapattinam (35k peak in 1050AD) on the Coromandel coast, Tirunelveli (30k in 1526AD), Senji (28k in 1526AD) and Kannur (26,57k in 1526AD) [@Careem2024Goddesses; @S2021Historical].
4. Antiquarian ports and local market nodes (10k to 25k inhabitants): Kaveripattinam (Poompuhar, 32k in 300AD before early mediaeval decline), Pattanam (22k in 300AD), Korkai (18k in 300AD), Arikamedu (10k in 300AD) and hundreds of market centres (*nagaram*) distributed across inland agrarian tracts [@Mathar2025Echoes; @Trouillet2017Hindu; @Allchin1995Archaeology].

# Limitations

Demographic reconstruction across Tamil Nadu and Kerala between 300AD and 1526AD is subject to several historical and preservation constraints:
1. Epigraphic survivorship bias: over 80% of surviving stone inscriptions record tax exemptions for Brahmanical *brahmadeyas* and Saiva or Vaishnava temple foundations (*devadana*), resulting in superior documentation for irrigated river valleys compared to dryland peasant communities (*vellanvagai*) and upland tribal settlements [@Mala2025Agricultur; @Gunasekaran2026Power].
2. Coastal geomorphological changes and port siltation: ancient ports such as Kaveripattinam, Arikamedu and Korkai suffered from extensive deltaic siltation and coastal subsidence, rendering continuous archaeological excavation of urban domestic architecture challenging [@S2021Historical]. In Kerala, the great Periyar flood of 1341AD altered the estuarine landscape, silting up the ancient harbour of Kodungallur (Muziris) while opening the deep-water inlet at Kochi [@Rita2022River].
3. Modern urban overbuilding: historical metropolises such as Madurai, Kanchipuram, Tiruchirappalli and Kozhikode have experienced continuous occupation for over two millennia, with modern civic infrastructure directly overlaying mediaeval archaeological deposits [@Kumar2024Architectu].
4. Administrative boundary fluidity: historical territorial units (*nadu*, *kottam*, *valanadu*, *mandalam*) underwent periodic redrawing under competing dynastic administrations, requiring spatial harmonisation against modern catchment boundaries [@Bes2022Sources].

# Conclusion

Between 300AD and 1526AD, Tamil Nadu and Kerala sustained unbroken demographic expansion, growing from 5,10M inhabitants during late antiquity to 12,80M by the dawn of the early modern era across 167.458 km² of peninsular territory. This demographic resilience was underpinned by two distinct regional modes of environmental adaptation: in Tamil Nadu, the construction of cascading tank chains (*eri*) in dry uplands and canal networks across the Kaveri delta, supervised by village assemblies (*ur*, *sabha*) and financed through temple estates; in Kerala, intensive multi-tier tree horticulture and wet-rice cultivation along coastal lagoons, integrated into trans-oceanic Indian Ocean commerce.

The historical trajectory demonstrates that southern South Asia maintained substantial demographic density through successive political transitions, including the decline of the Sangam chiefdoms, the rise of the Pallava and Pandya kingdoms, the hegemony of the Imperial Cholas, the disruptions of the Madurai Sultanate, and the agrarian reorganisation of the Vijayanagara Empire. The clearing of interior drylands and the adoption of deep-well multi-cropping under Nayaka administration laid the agricultural foundations for the demographic expansion of early modern South India.

# Appendix

The INDUS source ledger catalogues 3.855 primary settlements across three sub-regions (1.879 in Pallava Tondaimandalam, Chola Kaveri and Kongu; 1.045 in Chera Perumal, Venad and Calicut Malabar; and 931 in Pandya Nadu and the southern Tamil plains), reconciled against official census gazetteers, multi-repository archaeological survey inventories and epigraphic registers. Table \ref{tab:saturation} details the four-wave saturation audit across 4.655 candidate localities demonstrating comprehensive regional coverage.

```{r tbl-saturation, results='asis'}
sat_waves <- led_data$saturation_audit$waves
sat_rows <- lapply(sat_waves, function (w) {
  data.frame(
    Wave = paste0("Wave ", w$wave),
    SourceClass = clean_text(w$source_class),
    PriorTotal = viscount_fmt_number(as.numeric(w$prior_cumulative_included), 0L),
    NewlyIncluded = viscount_fmt_number(as.numeric(w$newly_included), 0L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_sat <- do.call(rbind, sat_rows)
viscount_table(
  df_sat,
  "Four-wave asymptotic saturation audit of catalogued settlements across Tamil Nadu and Kerala.",
  c("Ingestion Wave", "Source Category", "Prior Cumulative", "Newly Included"),
  list(label = "tab:saturation", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```
